name: Future Making & Creativity
description:
The slogan “everything is interconnected” has gained widespread resonance in recent years. For some, it emerges from spiritual traditions or engagements with Eastern philosophies. Others encounter it through the study of quantum physics, systems theory, or process philosophy. Still others arrive at this insight through patterns observed in everyday life. While such ideas were once confined to the esoteric margins of Western thought, today even fields grounded in empirical science increasingly acknowledge the entangled, relational, and distributed nature of life, agency, and planetary transformation.

Scientific paradigms are shifting: “nature” is no longer understood solely as a mechanistic system to be governed or predicted, but increasingly as a complex assemblage of dynamic, distributed, and emerging relationships - systems in which humans are not merely participants, but also constitutive elements. Historically, science often sought to develop increasingly refined analytical tools to examine such patterns in human relations with nonhuman entities, thereby frequently reinforcing an ontological separation between humans and the world they observe. As a response, more-than-human studies aim to challenge these anthropocentric assumptions and illuminate the multiple, often subtle ways in which human life is entangled with ecological, social, and multispecies systems.

Yet a persistent epistemological and affective question remains: How can we come to “know” what lies beyond our sensory and cognitive capacities? How might we relate to beings and processes whose temporalities, chemistries, and intelligences do not align with human perception? And just as importantly, how might we become aware of the unconscious scripts, shadows, and resistances that shape our relationships with the more-than-human world?

This experimental laboratory investigates these questions by integrating artistic and ethnographic methodologies to engage with more-than-human worlds. Students will critically examine... (see document attached)
prerequisites:
Students of all disciplines are admitted to this course, but a good knowledge of English and an interest in practical creative work, and in fundamental questions of sustainability and impact are basic prerequisites for participation. 

The willingness to read scientific literature is also an important prerequisites, as their knowledge and application will influence the final grade. 

Important: You do not have to have previous experience with artistic or ethnographic methods. General interest in the topic and eagerness to learn will be sufficient.
